🤖 The hidden cost could be message inflation.

Customer:

> “What’s the price?”



A poorly designed bot:

> Hi 👋
Thanks for contacting us.
Which product are you interested in?
Here are our options.
Would you like to know more?
Shall I connect you with an expert?



One customer question.

Six outbound messages.

At scale, the conversation itself becomes a cost centre.

And AI could make this even more interesting.

LLM-powered bots can explain, clarify, confirm and follow up — sometimes when one concise message would have done the job.

So perhaps the new metric shouldn't just be:

CPL | CAC | Conversion Rate

It should also be:

Messages per resolved conversation.

But there is another piece of the puzzle.

👨‍💼 Humans vs 🤖 API

A salesperson manually replying through the WhatsApp Business App/Web isn't the same thing as sending through the WhatsApp Business Platform/API.

The October pricing change applies to the Platform.

That's where WhatsApp Co-Existence becomes interesting.

Co-Existence allows the same number to remain active in the WhatsApp Business App while also being connected to the Cloud API, with Business App conversations available in the connected business inbox.

So a potential architecture becomes:

Ad / Lead
↓
🤖 API → automated qualification
↓
🎯 High-intent lead
↓
👨‍💼 Human → WhatsApp Business App/Web
↓
🤝 Conversation → conversion

Instead of forcing the entire customer journey through the API.

The question changes.

Not:

“AI or human?”

But:

“Which part of the conversation actually needs the API?”

Use API automation for:

• Lead qualification
• FAQs
• Routing
• Notifications
• CRM workflows
• Repetitive tasks

And let humans take over when context, negotiation, trust or closing matter more than automation.

There's another lesson for CRM selection.

Don't ask:

> “Does your CRM integrate with WhatsApp?”



Ask:

> “Does it support WhatsApp Co-Existence, and can Business App conversations sync back into the CRM?”



Because if it doesn't, your team may end up conducting the entire conversation through the Platform — changing the economics of every additional message.

📊 Start measuring:

Cost per resolved conversation.

Not just cost per message.

Because the smartest chatbot may not be the one that says the most.

It may be the one that knows when to stop talking — and when to hand the conversation to a human. 🤯

content:
“Looking for a freelancer to build our complete ERP.”

I’ve been seeing more posts like this on LinkedIn—founders looking for one person to turn an ambitious business vision into a working platform.

Sometimes it’s a small, clearly defined project. Sometimes the scope sounds like an entire technology department’s responsibility.

Some posts may simply be conversation starters. But if the intention is to build, expectations deserve a reality check.

There’s a saying: “Horses for courses.”
It applies just as much to IT and AI solutions.

There are exceptional freelancers who build excellent products. For a prototype, a focused application, a specialist integration or a well-defined MVP, an experienced independent professional can be exactly the right choice.

But consider what “build an ERP” might actually involve:
• Understanding how different departments operate—and where their processes conflict.
• Designing permissions, approvals, audit trails and data controls.
• Migrating existing records and integrating other systems.
• Testing exceptions, failures and real-world usage.
• Managing deployment, training, maintenance and business continuity.

Someone has to own every one of those responsibilities.
When the budget excludes a responsibility, that responsibility doesn’t disappear. It often lands on the founder.
You may find yourself becoming the business analyst, product manager, tester and support coordinator—while also trying to run your company.

AI can help an experienced developer deliver more. It can accelerate implementation considerably. But the business decisions, validation and accountability still need owners.
A working demonstration is a milestone. Running payroll, inventory, purchasing or production reliably is an ongoing commitment.

Before choosing a freelancer, an internal team or a development partner, ask:
→ Is this an experiment, an MVP or a system my business will depend on?
→ Who will challenge incomplete requirements and identify missing workflows?
→ Who will independently test whether it works?
→ What happens when the person building it is unavailable?
→ Who owns support and improvements after launch?

An agency label alone doesn’t answer these questions either. Ask for evidence of capability, continuity and delivery.

After 20 years of building software with founders and businesses, my advice is simple:
If your budget is small, make the first version smaller. Keep the responsibilities visible.
A capable freelancer may be the right answer. A small team may be the right answer. A long-term technology partner may be the right answer.

Match the choice to the complexity, business risk and support the project requires.

The question worth asking is:
“What will it take to build this—and keep it working when my business depends on it?”
